speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Welcome to The Product Podcast, Wade.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Awesome. Thanks for having me, Carlos.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I've been using your product since the early days, and I feel like you're one of those gladiators that finds a way to stay alive. Because every single time I see the news that OpenAI or Anthropic released a new variation of the LLMs, a bunch of startups die, but somehow you keep finding ways to stay alive.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Yeah, at least with the algorithms right now, we kind of seesaw back and forth between the "it's over" and "we're so back" mentality. A lot of that just feels like the algorithms and the headlines yanking things around a little bit. Our approach has always just been to wake up every day, listen to our customers, and figure out how to ship things that make their lives better. And I think if you do that over the course of decades, your chances are pretty decent that you're going to still find a way to be in business.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think there are a few unique facts about your business. First of all, you guys are fully remote, right?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: We are.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: And you are profitable, which is a rare thing to see these days.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: We are profitable as well. From No-Code to a Code Product

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Tell me more about that repositioning or expansion you had to make in your product to make sure you're incorporating all of these new AI capabilities.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Zapier grew up in the no-code era. A lot of folks credit us with being one of the pioneers of that stuff. Mostly the approach was, how do we take a lot of the burden of creating automations off humans who don't know how to write code? Let's make it easy for them. So for the longest time, that was putting UI abstractions on top of APIs, trying to make these simple point-and-click tools that took away the toil that someone who didn't know how to write code had to do to build these automations and integrations. You fast-forward to 2022, 2023, ChatGPT launches. I wouldn't say that was the first true wakeup call. We were like, "Wow, this is a really impressive product," for sure. But for us, the power really dawned on us at the GPT-4 launch, which happened about six months later. GPT-4 was a much better model than ChatGPT launched with. It was a lot cheaper, and the fact that it launched only six months later felt to us like a sign that there was about to be this exponential curve of improvements with these models. So we thought, well, if that's the case, what needs to change about Zapier? And it felt like there were two really important dimensions. First, the product needs to change: we need to bake these capabilities into the core experience. Second, how we work has to change: these tools can help us be more productive, work better. Initially this was a period of quite a bit of exploration inside Zapier, where we were trying a whole bunch of new capabilities, shipping things inside the product, changing how we worked. But by and large, I'm trying to think, how many of those experiments actually survived? Most of them actually didn't. The turning point really happened about a year ago, when Opus 4 or 5, GPT-5, whatever came out, I forget the names, it's hard to keep track, but these were really sophisticated reasoning models. And we saw all of a sudden that, at least internally, these things were one-shotting writing code. And we're like, oh, okay, it's really here. Our engineers weren't reading the code anymore. They were just prompting the model, the model would write it, they'd have some tests or evals to check its work, but by and large not reading the code. And that was finally the first moment where we were like, ah, we know how the product can change from here. Where it once was that no-code was about abstracting away the toil of working with code, we realized, okay, Zapier is actually going to write the code for you. So now, when you look at what's growing the fastest inside Zapier, it's Zapier MCP. And the reason it's growing so fast is you can install it into your agent of choice, and then the agent goes and builds the automations for you, and it writes them with code. So Zapier is a code-based product now, even though the users aren't. It's like having the world's best developer sitting right next to you, and you just tell them, "Hey, can you build an automation for this? Can you connect this to that?" And all of a sudden it brings to life a lot of the original vision of Zapier, which was to make automation work for everyone. It turns out the best no-code product was always just an agent writing code for you in the first place. Why the Labs Can't Crack It

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: It's so funny, because you're right, your product is more technical than ever, yet your main customer is still the non-technical user. So my question is, okay, you make this MCP work, and now people can use your product from other interfaces. Why can't OpenAI or Anthropic crack that code? They keep releasing their own variations of automation workflows, yet yours seems to be the winner.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I think there's a product truism here, which is that a focused team on a very specific set of problems is always going to be a little bit ahead of a team working on more general capabilities. OpenAI and Anthropic are building these incredible models and capabilities. They've got some amazing applications on top of them, but they also build a lot of stuff that doesn't work on the application side. And they're quite large companies now too. So the things they really care about are going to be excellent, aka the models. The models just continue to get better and better. But I still believe there's a huge amount of room for entrepreneurs to build on top of those capabilities and extend what they can do into specialized domains, unique use cases, novel UIs or user experiences alongside them that won't come from the labs. For every entrepreneur I talk to, it's somewhat of a scary time, because you think, "Are they just going to eat everything we do?" But you can come back and pay attention to where they're innovating and say, "How do we go alongside them instead of in front of them?" You can build capabilities that continue to be complementary over time. I wish I had a silver bullet to propose to folks, "If you do this, you'll always have a complementary product." But what I see the best companies do is they're very quick at rewriting their priors. When new model capabilities come out, they're willing to just say, "Okay, throw this experiment away, this doesn't matter anymore, let's shift over to this thing, because this is where it's all going to work." And if you can build a community of customers who appreciate your orientation, you'll always be at least a step ahead on that specific dimension. You may not be on this other set of things, but the thing this group of customers cares about, you can make sure to have the best thing in the world for them.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: That reminds me of something someone said a long time ago, that there are two kinds of strategies. One is trying to build your product against the models, betting you can have an edge and do something better than the models. The other is to assume the models are going to get so much better that you have to work alongside them. And I think that's similar to what you're saying: assuming the models keep getting better, and then picking where you can really add the value.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Yeah, that's what it really boils down to. You have to pick where you think there are places you can extend on top of them. This requires you to really understand how these models advance. You've got to understand the bitter lesson really well. The common trope is, how do you build product capabilities that get better with new model releases, not get wiped out by new model capabilities? That's the fork you're trying to thread when making these decisions. Building Agent-First

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Another thing I want to explore is this concept of being agent-first. As more and more agents use the web and the tools, there are now more agents out there than humans using those products. So how are you adjusting your product to make sure this new kind of user is making the most out of it?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I think we're starting to see that agents are really, truly going to be the new computing platform. In the last couple of months, we've seen these new consumer agent products come out and gain a huge amount of popularity, and OpenAI and Anthropic launched their versions of it too. These are products where humans are basically delegating their computing work to these agents, and the agents go and act on their behalf. To me, that opens up a new computing paradigm. In the past it was, "We've got an operating system, let's build software for the operating system." Then it was browsers, "Let's build capabilities for browsers." Then you had mobile, "Let's build that for mobile." So to me it's yet another extension of that. We've got agents, so what are the tools that agents need available to them to do well? A really interesting way to think about your opportunity is, here's what these agents can do today, here's what they kind of stink at. Do you think the models or the harnesses are going to eventually build those capabilities? If no, then there's a really interesting product idea, where you can say, "I'm going to build a product that the agent can reach for." The agent should be able to sign up for it, buy it, do everything a human should be able to do using that product. And if you do that, I think you've built a product that is effectively agent-first. Don't Build an Agent, Have the Agent Build a Workflow

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So as you build your own agent-first product and try to be as agnostic in terms of tools and models as possible, how did you go about making those cost decisions to make sure people are making the best possible decision and not getting slapped in the face with a huge bill at the end?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: That's tricky right now, because there's definitely a lot of expensive usage going on. One of the things we encourage all our customers to do is, a lot of times they're building agents when they should just be having the agent build a workflow. We see this ourselves. Instead of asking a bot, or asking whatever your agent tool is, to go build an automation, build a routine for you, have it go build this app for you. And Zaps run deterministically, which means they're much, much cheaper. In fact, some benchmarks show they're about 71% cheaper. The reason is it's a far more cost-effective, reliable, and efficient way to run most workflows, versus having an agent wake up every time and reason over the instructions every single time. So that's one way you can reduce your overall token spend. The second thing, and this is where it starts to get a little more technical, is you can use routers. A lot of folks these days have a frontier model route tasks to a cheaper model, so they might send it to Haiku, or an open-source model, or a smaller decision model. As a result, that can help them reduce the overall cost of the workflow on tasks where they don't actually need frontier intelligence. Of course, the trick is that a lot of less technical folks immediately nope out of that discussion. They're like, "That sounds complicated." So this is why I think the best AI products have a real wedge in helping with these cost-optimization decisions: how does the product just do that for you? And this is where I do think there's a fair amount of innovation entrepreneurs can have, because they're not incumbent to run these tasks on one model family. You don't have to just run it on the Anthropic models or just the OpenAI models. You can use a whole ensemble of models to reduce the overall cost of running the application, and in some cases not use models at all. You can write code, you can have deterministic tasks go. So there are real advantages when you're able to use models from a whole ecosystem of providers. That's another place where entrepreneurs have an opportunity to build products that are advantaged over what the labs can provide. Getting Into Large Enterprises

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I would say probably not just entrepreneurs, but even in large enterprises. I'm curious to know how you're getting into those large accounts, because traditionally the API was meant for the indie hacker who was automating a bunch of things, and now you're targeting a bunch of larger enterprises. So what's the use case for the folks who maybe don't have all the decision-making power?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Yeah. A few years back, we spent a lot of time addressing gaps on our underlying platform. Zapier very much was a solo-user product, really best in a small business. So we spent a lot of time launching a lot of the checkbox features: SSO, SCIM, audit logging, all that sort of stuff. A lot of that got addressed. But the real thing was getting really good at the thing that makes this product category scary. For a lot of products, you have your checkbox features, but then there's usually one or two features that make a CIO go, "Oh." If you have a meeting recorder, it's like, "Well, how are you handling privacy?" And all of a sudden that's like, "I get that you love this product, but there's some dimension that freaks the CIO out." For our product category, that's all these connectors. If you connect these, where's the data going? Who's able to send it where? All of a sudden that makes this product category one that's like, "It's cool that you can do this, but you might also shoot this whole business in the foot." So we spent a lot of time building governance systems on top of the connectors to make sure that if you're a CIO, if you're a leader responsible for how data moves through an organization, you can now actually have incredible visibility into who has access to what. Can you turn on read access to this system, write access to that system, the permission level? And Zapier is even more fine-grained than you often get out of OAuth natively. As a result, it takes this thing that's a scary proposition and says, "Hey, if you actually standardize on Zapier with your connectors, you're going to have way more ability to see and govern how humans access this data, how agents access this data, than you would with any other capability out there." That, to me, is how you flip what might seem like a scary thing in a product category into a strength. We invested a lot in making sure that's really strong. So now we hear from, I can think of a very large Fortune 500 company that went from saying, "We're kind of nervous about this" to now saying, "Hey, we do not let any connector or automation run on any system other than Zapier." And that even goes for native integrations, because they just trust they have way more visibility into what's going on when they use our platform versus something else. So what it really took was understanding not just the check-the-box stuff, we're great at all that too, but how do you actually address the thing that really is the fear an organization has in your product category? Governance as the Next Enterprise Frontier

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think that's the next big frontier in enterprise. A lot of players are trying to become that control tower, or an agentic interface to connect all their different applications. Because you're right, today a lot of these enterprises are still using AI assistants for basic use cases, such as fixing typos. But the actual connection between other tools to automate work is still something that's not happening, mostly because of fear.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Spot on. And I do empathize with the leaders in this position, because you're somewhat caught between a rock and a hard place. You really feel like you have one or two options. One is to turn all this stuff on and let your team go wild building all these capabilities, which in the short term feels very powerful, you can do all this incredible stuff, but you're opening up all these risk vectors that are eventually going to bite you. Or you say no to all of it, and you basically shut down innovation in your organization, nothing gets done, and the best people who want to be the most AI-forward start leaving. So you're stuck between these two worlds where neither feels particularly good. And for some of the companies struggling the most with this, it gets even harder because it gets caught up in a committee. So now they sit around a room talking about it versus actually doing anything. This is where the application layer can really solve some problems for folks and say, "Hey, we've got a mechanism that lets you put common-sense, smart governance tools in place that allow you to get the best innovation you can on top of it, and close the worst risk vectors." So you get this third option that's like, "Ah, that's kind of what folks have been looking for." That's where we've put a lot of our effort, finding that mechanism where someone can come in and say yes to a lot of people being able to build and create automations, do a lot of the things they want their employees to be able to do, but shut down the most risky behaviors that tend to pop up. Agents That Recommend Your Next Automation

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: If we assume for a second that we're an organization that already figured out governance, and now people are empowered to start creating some of these agentic workflows, a challenge I see is discovery. They might not know what tools to use to accomplish a certain task. So how do we have AI help you figure this out?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I think this is a really interesting area to work on. One thing I've noticed for myself, and folks should stay tuned on this dimension because I think we'll launch some capabilities around this, is I've set up agents that are watching me work now. It goes and looks over all the logs I'm emitting from my agent sessions, from Slack, Gmail, calendar, docs, code, data, and it's literally saying, "Here's the task that you're doing every single week." Then once a week it wakes up and says, "Hey, here are some ways I could have helped you this week." We've worked on automation recommendations for years pre-AI, and honestly, we never really could do things that were all that good. The recommendations felt kind of sterile and bland, and as a result I don't think they ever really worked. I remember it was always kind of the common joke: a new product manager or a new designer would come in and be like, "Why don't we work on the recommendation system?" And honestly, I'd come a little jaded about it. I was just like, "I don't think it's going to work, I've just never seen it work." So people kept taking their swing, kept taking their swing, and it just didn't work. But this agent-first version of it, literally the hacky version on my desktop, was better than any of the sophisticated versions we'd built in the no-code era. So I think there's a real opportunity to actually have agents be the ones that start to make recommendations for you. Now, it has some of the challenges we've been talking about: you have to be comfortable giving agents the ability to watch all the stuff you do, and that's going to set off all sorts of flags for a company to say, "How do we launch that capability safely?" That's where I say, stay tuned, I think we've got some ideas coming. But if it's just you, I'd say literally just go prompt your agent and say, "Hey, look at all the work I've done over the last week and propose automations for me, propose things you could have taken off my plate," and see what it suggests. I think you'll find that even that alone gives you some pretty good recommendations for where to start.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Honestly, that's what I've been doing for myself: the classic AI meeting note-taker, and then the agent of choice scanning through my docs. But it's just for me. I can't wait to have a more holistic view of how people are doing work, not just to spy on them, but to actually help them do work better.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: It's remarkable how well it works. Even just the basic version of the prompt. This is the kind of stuff where you do just see the models get better and better. They're incredible. Structuring the Day: No Meetings Before 11

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So I want to talk about you as a CEO builder. Your company is really big, and you seem to be still in the weeds building with the team. Tell me a little more about how you structure your day.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I've definitely gotten better at it, or found my groove for how it works, in part because as the organization scaled up, I fell into the common trap of being in meetings back-to-back all day, and then getting to the end of the day thinking, "What have I actually achieved?" I've talked to a bunch of people and ostensibly delegated out a bunch of work that's going to get done some way somehow, but it left me feeling not incredibly satisfied. And truth be told, we have a lot of talented people in the company who could have done those things without me. They didn't really need me for that stuff. The thing I started to think about, and this happened after I had kids, it made me think, I need to be spending a lot more time in maker mode, because I don't think I'll be able to stay up to date on what the models are capable of, what the application trends are, if I'm not spending time building myself. So honestly, I just told my assistant, "Hey, I don't want meetings before 11am. I'm just not going to do that." That way I tend to do my best heads-down time first thing in the morning. I usually have a couple of hours in the morning where I'm playing, building, thinking, mostly building, mostly prompting these days. That helps me get a feel for where these things are good, where they're not so good. It's not a panacea, this stuff is moving so stinking fast that I still constantly feel like I'm not as up to speed as I'd wish. But it's helping, and I can't imagine how out of touch I'd be if I kept operating in that back-to-back meeting mode all day, every day. So carving out a dedicated maker session every day for a couple of hours in the morning has been the big unlock for me. Fighting Meeting Inertia

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Are there any changes you've made to allow other managers to get the same type of feeling?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: This is very hard to do. I've found that at a certain amount of scale, I don't know what it is about organizations, I don't think it's humans, I think it's the organizational tendency to just add and add and add more meetings. And we're very bad at subtracting. So I feel like I kind of have to wake up every day and fight inertia and say, "No, we don't need that recurring meeting." We've tried various practices over the years where we put people on meeting quotas, a certain amount of meetings a week. One-on-ones are one of those things. I've certainly adjusted: I used to do one-on-ones every single week, and now I rarely do one-on-ones with my direct reports. I think that works better for CEOs, though, because you're mostly working with highly competent, highly skilled folks who don't need a lot of week-to-week career coaching and can problem-solve in a team meeting or async in Slack really effectively. So I don't know if that works for every role, but for my role it works really well. We've definitely done some spring-cleaning stuff. We've never gone as far as Shopify, which I think at the beginning of the year nuked all internal recurring meetings and said, "If it's worthwhile, it will come back." We do a tiny version of that. Honestly, we probably should try the bigger version of it. But more than any of these particular tactics, it really is just about continuing to walk the walk yourself. I push back on meetings all the time. "I don't think I need to be at this," or "I don't think this needs to exist," or "These two meetings, it's the same group of people plus or minus one person talking about the same thing, you should combine them, why are you doing this?" And just constantly telling folks, "Protect your time, protect your time," because attention is really scarce right now. If we find ourselves stuck in committee logjam, we're going to get steamrolled by somebody who's way more AI-first, agent-first, who's just going to have the agent go build the thing, and in the time it takes you to talk about it, they'll have the whole thing done. So you have to constantly remind people that's what's happening here. And I think if you do that well, you start to see more and more antibodies build up inside the organization against some of these more traditional organizational practices.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Half smiling, half crying as I hear you give this answer, because I'm there still, trying to remove myself from meetings, archive Slack channels, ask people to do the same, and meetings somehow keep popping up. I don't know what it is that makes people feel fulfilled in some way by it. I actually think AI could be an amazing helper for this: the same way it can look at how people are doing work and help them do it more efficiently, it could look at how people are spending time and give them ideas on how to optimize. The New Kind of Meeting That's Actually Valuable

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I agree. I would also say there's this odd new thing happening where, because of meeting recorders and how well the models do with lots of messy context, meetings can also be a really effective prompt for the model. You can literally get on a call and debate a feature and say, "I'm worried about this, this, and this," or "I think these capabilities will be excellent, these architecture decisions make a ton of sense." You just banter back and forth, and then take the transcript, fire off an agent, and say, "Hey, go build what we talked about." I'm finding that to work really, really well. So it's this funky situation where there's a new type of meeting that actually feels incredibly valuable, which is a vibrant debate over how to build something or why to build something, that elicits this really rich context for an agent. So meeting culture is hard, I guess, is where I net out on a lot of this. Closing the Loop and Giving Agents Broad Context

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think you're touching on something interesting that involves both meetings and all kinds of work, which is this opportunity of closing the loop: making sure you're gathering enough information and then having the AI be able to fix things without a lot of oversight. So how are you thinking about that, not just for meetings, but in general for the automations and workflows you're creating?

speaker: Wade Foster
text: The architecture we're finding is that the more context you can give these agents, the wider read access to raw data, not just summarized data but raw access to the database, the code, the Slack, the meeting notes, the messier the better, the better results you get out of it. It's able to sift over all of that stuff and deliver remarkably good capabilities. I think you have to be careful about how you give it write access to various tools, you do need to be thoughtful about that. You still figure out where you put humans in the loop, how you have good checks on what it can and cannot do. But by and large, broad-based read access to a lot of tools seems to make the agent give better outputs at the end of the day. The Self-Improving Company

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I had this interview with the CEO of Replit, and he was talking about the self-improving company, and how we're going to see more and more companies leverage this capability to improve much faster.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: I 100% agree with him. We've seen a number of folks talk about this, Jack talked about this at Square too. But it definitely feels like you're going to be able to create these feedback loops that the agents are constantly listening to, whether they're listening to customer complaints on social, customer calls, customer support tickets, or watching performance dashboards for how the application is doing. All of these things are generating signal around what is working and what is not. And then if you've got these goals set up for the agent, the agents can constantly be working on improving in those dimensions. So it definitely feels like this is the direction things are heading.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Wade, it's been a pleasure to have you on the pod. Thanks so much for being here with us.

speaker: Wade Foster
text: Awesome. Thank you for having me, Carlos. Pleasure's all mine.
